questions.question: What is T in identity<T>(value: T): T?
options: A runtime class you can new.
A type parameter the caller (or inference) fills in.
A runtime value you can call typeof T on.
questions.explanation: A generic is a function between types. You instantiate it; you do not new T.

reference.book: Effective TypeScript, 2nd Edition by Dan Vanderkam

questions.question: What does TypeScript infer for identity("a")?
options: T is "a" only if you used let, not a string argument.
Inference fails; you must write identity<string>("a").
questions.explanation: The argument proves T. Prefer inference over spelling the type argument.

questions.question: What does keyof T mean?
options: The union of T’s property names.
Object.keys at runtime as a type.
questions.explanation: For { name: string; age: number }, keyof T is "name" | "age".

questions.question: Can you switch (T) inside identity<T>?
options: Yes. T is still present at runtime as a constructor argument.
No. Types are erased. T is not a value.
questions.explanation: There is no way to ask what T is at runtime. Pass a runtime tag if you need that.

options: A function: it takes type parameters and produces a type.

questions.explanation: You instantiate a generic type the way you call a function, but in type space.

questions.question: Why write K extends keyof T instead of key: string?
options: string keys always type-check, so it is shorter.
It keeps obj[key] typed as T[K] and rejects unknown names.
questions.explanation: key: string would make obj[key] a wide type and allow typos.

questions.question: Is <T,> needed on an arrow in a .tsx file?
options: A trailing comma in <T,> tells TSX it is a type parameter, not a tag.
questions.explanation: TSX would parse <T> as a component. The trailing comma disambiguates.
